definition: Cedar shake roof replacement removes aging cedar shakes and shingles to the deck and installs new cedar over a ventilated nailing base. It renews a wood covering that relies on underlying airflow to resist rot and prolong service life, applying when moisture-driven cupping, splitting, and rot end a cedar roof past its service life rather than when individual split shakes can be patched.

signs: A cedar roof at or past its service life signals replacement, because cedar shake lasts 20 to 40 years and cedar shingle 30 to 50 years, per the Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau, with the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart listing wood at 25 years and maintenance setting where in the range a cedar roof lands.

Widespread cupping and warping across the cedar field indicates advanced moisture cycling, the dominant cedar failure mode, because moisture-driven cupping and warping degrade a cedar roof faster than insects, per Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau and NRCA guidance.

Edge splitting and cracked shakes across more than 25 to 30% of the roof crosses the contractor-consensus area threshold that favors replacement over continued spot repair, per industry repair-vs-replace guidance.
A shake that cracks under light bending fails the cedar flex test, the InterNACHI sign of advanced degradation regardless of surface appearance, per the InterNACHI flex-test guidance.

Moss and algae buildup with rot beneath cupped shakes indicates trapped moisture, the condition that accelerates on north-facing and shaded slopes where a cedar roof dries slowly, per Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau guidance.

A spongy or sagging roof deck under the cedar indicates moisture-rotted sheathing from years of trapped water beneath the wood, a structural condition that points toward replacement rather than a surface patch, per GAF inspection guidance.
Daylight through the roof deck seen from inside the attic indicates holes in the decking and the cedar field, a sign that points toward replacement rather than a patch, per This Old House.
selectionCriteria: Verify the contractor holds New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, a registration NOT a license (NJ issues no roofing license), with the 13VH registration number displayed on the contract and advertising per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144.
Confirm $500,000-per-occurrence commercial general liability coverage required by N.J.S.A. 56:8-142, verified by a certificate of insurance, before any tear-off begins.
Require a written contract for any home-improvement work over $500 under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2 and an itemized written estimate that sets scope, labor, materials, and timeline before work begins.

Confirm the cedar selection by type and fire class is presented in writing — hand-split shake, sawn shingle, and fire-retardant-treated cedar at a Class B or Class C product class per the Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau Certi-Guard program.

Confirm the contractor will strip the cedar to the bare deck rather than roof over it, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 prohibits roofing over wood shake and over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck, and will install a ventilated nailing base holding at least 1.5 inches of drying air space per Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau install guidance.
Ask for a written workmanship warranty on the labor, separate from the manufacturer material warranty on the cedar, plus documented assessment and local references.

technicalFacts.fact: Cedar shake lasts 20 to 40 years and cedar shingle 30 to 50 years; the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart lists a single 'Wood' row at 25 years, and maintenance sets where in the range a cedar roof lands because moisture cycling drives most premature cedar failure.
technicalFacts.source: Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau and InterNACHI (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: A cedar roof needs at least 1.5 inches of drying air space beneath the shakes from a ventilated nailing base; the ventilation extends cedar service life and slows the moisture-driven cupping, splitting, and rot that end most cedar roofs.
technicalFacts.source: Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau install guidance (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Untreated cedar shakes and shingles are nonclassified on their own under UL 790 and ASTM E108; pressure-impregnated fire-retardant cedar carries a Class B or Class C product class; a Class A wood roof is achieved only as a tested assembly of fire-retardant shakes over a fire-retardant cap sheet, not from the wood covering alone.
technicalFacts.source: Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau Certi-Guard program; UL 790 / ASTM E108 (per gold and fact pack §7)

technicalFacts.fact: A new cedar roof cannot go over an old cedar roof; N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 (NJ Rehabilitation Subcode) prohibits roofing over wood shake and over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck, so a cedar replacement requires a full tear-off to the deck. The NJ subcode expressly lists wood shake, unlike the model IRC R908.3.1.1.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4, NJ Uniform Construction Code (per gold and fact pack §6)

technicalFacts.fact: A complete tear-off and replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, no inspection, and no notice to the construction official; a commercial cedar roof or a structural change to rafters or trusses still triggers a permit (the ordinary-maintenance exemption on a commercial building covers only repair of up to 25% of total roof area in a 12-month period).
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, NJ Uniform Construction Code (per gold and fact pack §6)

technicalFacts.fact: A full tear-off exposes the deck for inspection and replacement of plywood or OSB rotted under the old cedar from years of trapped moisture; the contractor-consensus 25-to-30% area threshold and the InterNACHI flex test (a shake that cracks under light bending) are the signs of advanced degradation that favor replacement over spot repair.
technicalFacts.source: InterNACHI flex-test guidance and industry repair-vs-replace guidance (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Newark crosses the 32 degree F freezing point repeatedly through winter with an average January low near 25.5 degrees F; the freeze-thaw and moisture load drives the cupping, splitting, and rot that ends a cedar roof.
technicalFacts.source: NOAA 1991-2020 normals at Newark Liberty (EWR), with Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau and NRCA maintenance guidance (per gold)

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced NJ climate figures: "Essex County's 49 inches of annual rainfall, summer humidity averaging 70-80%" and "New Jersey's humidity accelerates cedar decay compared to the Pacific Northwest where western red cedar originates."
defabToKill.fix: Drop the invented 49-inch / 70-80% climate numbers. The only attributable climate figure is the NOAA 1991-2020 Newark Liberty (EWR) average January low near 25.5 degrees F driving freeze-thaw; frame moisture cycling as the dominant cedar failure mode per Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau and NRCA, not via fabricated rainfall/humidity stats.

defabToKill.issue: Fabricated material-specific lifespans: "Premium western red cedar shakes in Essex County last 25-35 years... Untreated shakes in shaded, humid locations may decline to 18-25 years. White cedar shakes... have a shorter 15-20 year lifespan." and "Cedar roofs that received regular treatment... can exceed 35 years. Neglected cedar roofs... may fail by year 20."
defabToKill.fix: Use the gold/CSSB ranges: cedar shake lasts 20 to 40 years and cedar shingle 30 to 50 years (Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau), with InterNACHI listing wood at 25 years, and maintenance setting where in the range a cedar roof lands. No invented western-red-vs-white-cedar sub-ranges.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced failure-mechanism claims stated as fact: "Splitting along the grain is normal weathering... Splitting across the grain indicates structural failure of the wood cells" and "Curling, cupping, and lifting... indicate loss of the natural oils that keep cedar flexible."
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the sourced signs: widespread cupping and warping = advanced moisture cycling (Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau / NRCA); a shake that cracks under light bending fails the InterNACHI flex test; edge splitting and cracked shakes over 25-30% of the field crosses the contractor-consensus replacement threshold.

defabToKill.issue: Invented whole-job dollar totals: "Premium western red cedar shake replacement runs $15,000-$28,000 installed"; "Material alone costs $300-$500 per square... installation labor at $350-$600 per square"; "Cedar shingle replacement... runs 15-20% less at $12,000-$22,000." The gold carries NO whole-job total for cedar.
defabToKill.fix: State the only gold-sourced figure: premium cedar runs $10 to $20-plus per square foot installed (NHI Contractors NJ pricing), above NJ asphalt $5.50-$11.00/sf (Josten Roofing) and below NJ slate $10-$30/sf. Hand-split shake costs more than sawn shingle (CSSB); fire-retardant cedar adds pressure-impregnation cost. Labor is ~60-70% of a wood-roof install and NJ sits 10-40% above national (Modernize/HomeGuide). No invented project total.

defabToKill.issue: Fabricated maintenance-cost economics: "Professional cleaning and preservative treatment every 3-5 years costs $800-$2,000. Moss treatment adds $300-$600. Over a 30-year life, maintenance totals $8,000-$15,000" and "the total 30-year cost of cedar ownership to $23,000-$43,000... individual shake replacements that average $200-$500 per visit." None of these are in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Delete the entire 30-year cost-of-ownership / maintenance-dollar table. Keep only the grounded driver: a ventilated nailing base (1.5 inches air space, CSSB) extends cedar life and slows moisture-driven cupping and rot; service life depends on maintenance because moisture cycling drives most premature cedar failure. No invented maintenance totals or per-visit figures.

defabToKill.issue: Brand-roster and fabricated synthetic/asphalt alternative pricing: "Synthetic cedar-look products from DaVinci, CertainTeed, and Brava... at $14,000-$24,000 installed, with zero maintenance and 50+ year lifespans" and "Architectural asphalt shingles in cedar-tone colors... at $9,000-$14,000 installed."
defabToKill.fix: Cut the DaVinci/CertainTeed/Brava brand roster and the invented synthetic/asphalt totals. If contrasting materials, use only the gold per-square-foot positioning: cedar $10-$20+/sf sits above NJ asphalt ($5.50-$11.00/sf, Josten Roofing) and below NJ slate ($10-$30/sf). No synthetic-product totals or brand-listed alternatives.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced deck-upgrade pricing and re-deck claim: "solid plywood decking must be installed over the skip sheathing, adding $2-$4 per square foot."
defabToKill.fix: Drop the $2-$4/sf figure. Ground the decking point in code: N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires complete removal of the cedar covering and replacement of deteriorated plywood or OSB; a full tear-off exposes the deck for inspection and repair. State that tear-off and deck repair add cost (gold pricing factor) without an invented per-sf number.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced install-method specifics stated as fact: "specific spacing between adjacent shakes (1/4 to 3/8 inch)"; "Stainless steel nails are mandatory... galvanized nails corrode in contact with cedar's tannic acids"; "Installation pace averages 2-4 squares per day per installer... 5-8 days of active installation."
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the gold-sourced method: install a ventilated nailing base holding at least 1.5 inches of drying air space, then lay new cedar to Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau install guidance so the wood roof drains and dries. Do not assert the 1/4-3/8 inch spacing, stainless-vs-galvanized tannic-acid claim, or the squares-per-day / 5-8 day duration unless CSSB guidance is cited for them; the gold does not carry them.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced weathering/patina and maintenance-program specifics: "New cedar shakes weather to a silver-gray patina within 6-12 months... apply UV-blocking preservative within the first 6 months"; "annual inspection, gutter cleaning twice yearly... professional preservative treatment every 3-5 years."
defabToKill.fix: Reframe the decision around the actual defining factor: a cedar roof's service life depends on the ventilated nailing base (1.5 inches air space, CSSB) and on moisture management, because moisture-driven cupping, splitting, and rot — accelerated by Essex County freeze-thaw (NOAA EWR) — end most cedar roofs. Drop the invented 6-12 month patina window, 6-month preservative deadline, and the specific every-3-5-year treatment cadence.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced fire/replacement framing absent any fire-class fact: the article omits the cedar fire-rating reality entirely while presenting itself as the decision overview.
defabToKill.fix: Center the position-3 decision on the two genuine decision factors the gold supports: (1) cedar fire class — untreated cedar is nonclassified under UL 790/ASTM E108, fire-retardant-treated cedar carries Class B or C as a product, and Class A wood is an assembly rating (CSSB Certi-Guard); and (2) the code requirement that cedar must be torn off to the deck, not roofed over (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 lists wood shake). These are the things a homeowner must understand before choosing cedar replacement.

parentDebtToAvoid: The gold credentialsHighlight chip reads 'NJ HIC Licensed' — NJ issues NO roofing license; write 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor' / 'registered NJ HIC' and never 'licensed' for NQR's credential.

Do NOT reproduce a synthetic-product or membrane brand roster (DaVinci/CertainTeed/Brava/GAF/Owens Corning) as NQR partnerships or certifications; brands may be named only as external data/guidance sources (e.g., GAF inspection guidance as a cited source).

Do NOT invent a single whole-job cedar replacement total — the gold substantiates only per-square-foot cedar pricing ($10-$20+/sf, NHI Contractors NJ), comparative material positioning, and labor-share/NJ-premium percentages; there is no gold-attributed project total.
Do NOT state any unsourced NJ climate figure (rainfall inches, humidity %); the only attributable climate number is the NOAA EWR average January low near 25.5 degrees F.

Frame warranty honestly as two parts — the manufacturer material warranty on the cedar (factory defects, preserved when installed to spec) and NQR's separate written workmanship warranty on the labor — never as a brand certification or 'Golden Pledge'-style program.

articleAngles.signs: The directAnswer names the cedar-specific replacement signals: a cedar roof at or past its 20-to-40-year shake / 30-to-50-year shingle service life (Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau), widespread cupping and warping from moisture cycling, edge splitting across more than 25 to 30% of the field, a shake that cracks under the InterNACHI flex test, moss with rot beneath cupped shakes, and a spongy or sagging deck or daylight through the decking — the signs that point past spot repair to full replacement.
articleAngles.costGuide: There is NO real whole-job total in the gold — answer per-square-foot only: premium cedar roofing in New Jersey runs $10 to $20-plus per square foot installed (NHI Contractors NJ pricing), placing it above NJ asphalt ($5.50-$11.00/sf, Josten Roofing) and below NJ slate ($10-$30/sf). Hand-split shake costs more than sawn shingle; fire-retardant cedar adds pressure-impregnation cost; labor is roughly 60-70% of a wood-roof install and NJ ranges sit 10-40% above national (Modernize/HomeGuide). Explicitly avoid any invented project total or maintenance-dollar table.
articleAngles.decision: The single most important thing a homeowner should understand is that cedar replacement is governed by two non-negotiable factors: cedar must be torn off to the deck rather than roofed over, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 (which expressly lists wood shake, unlike the model IRC) prohibits roofing over wood shake and over a deteriorated deck; and cedar's fire performance is a material trade-off — untreated cedar is nonclassified under UL 790/ASTM E108, fire-retardant-treated cedar carries only a Class B or Class C product class, and a Class A wood roof is achievable solely as a tested assembly (Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau Certi-Guard). The ventilated nailing base (at least 1.5 inches of drying air space) is what governs how long the new cedar lasts.
